strengths: Addresses an important optimization class with applications to sparse PCA, nonnegative PCA, and nonlinear eigenvalue problems.
The orthogonal row-block update correctly preserves XᵀX and applies to rectangular Stiefel matrices. Reducing two-row updates to rotations and reflections is a useful computational design.

The experiments cover four problem families, ten datasets, and multiple ranks and regularization parameters, with substantial reported objective improvements on several settings and relevant comparisons including ManPG and OptM.
weaknesses: The central stationarity claim in Theorem 5.5 is false under the stated assumptions. Consider n=r=3, X=I, f(X)=⟨A,X⟩ with A=[[0,0.5,-0.5],[-0.5,0,0.5],[0.5,-0.5,0]], and the convex row-separable function h(X)=Σ_i|Σ_j X_ij−1|. With Q=0, every two-row exact subproblem is minimized by I₂, yet the feasible curve exp(−tA) has objective derivative −1.5 at t=0. Thus an exact BS₂ point need not be critical. Appendix B.8 incorrectly turns the existence of a suitable subgradient for each block into the existence of one subgradient satisfying every block simultaneously.

The strong-convergence proof has independent substantive errors. Equation (56), step ②, exchanges Bᵗ and Bᵗ⁺¹ despite Xᵗ⁺¹ depending on Bᵗ. Lemma 6.6(b) also incorrectly converts a root-mean-square residual bound into a mean-residual bound: for n=3, r=1, k=2, h=0, f(x)=x₂, and x=e₁, its left side is 1 while its right side is √(2/3). These errors invalidate the presented proof of Theorem 6.8.

The exact breakpoint solver in Section 7.1 is incorrect as written. The substitution t=tan(θ) omits cos(θ)=0, which can contain global minimizers. Discarding coordinates with y_i=0 is also invalid for the ℓ₁ penalty: when x_i≠0, their contribution λ|x_i|/√(1+t²) depends on t. Consequently, the claimed exact subproblem solution is not guaranteed.

The experimental description contains a consequential feasibility inconsistency. Section 9.1 initializes nonnegative PCA with X(G_i,i)=1/|G_i|, giving column squared norm 1/|G_i| rather than 1. Since OBCD preserves the Gram matrix, this initialization cannot yield the reported near-machine-precision feasibility. The implementation must be reconciled with the stated procedure; the correct normalization is 1/√|G_i|.

The evaluation does not adequately isolate algorithmic superiority. Only the proposed breakpoint routine uses C++, and the baseline-plus-OBCD experiments receive ten additional seconds without an equal-budget baseline-continuation control. Baseline tuning, preprocessing, stopping tolerances, random seeds, and variability across repeated runs are insufficiently documented. Additional objective reduction alone does not establish stronger stationarity.

The demonstrated scope is narrower than the broad claims: all experiments use k=2 and n≤1000, without convincing scaling studies or ablations isolating reflections and exact subproblem optimization. Assumption 6.1 also excludes unbounded subdifferentials encountered at zeros for ℓ₀ penalties and at boundaries for nonnegativity indicators, limiting the strong-convergence coverage of headline applications.

Combining rotations and reflections, structured quadratic surrogates, and sampled working-set selection is a promising practical algorithm design.

Experiments cover four problem classes, ten datasets, multiple ranks and regularization strengths, and relevant baselines including ManPG and OptM. Several reported results show substantial improvements.
weaknesses: The central stationarity claim in Theorem 5.5 is false under the stated assumptions. Appendix B.8 incorrectly exchanges 'for every block, there exists a subgradient' with existence of one subgradient satisfying every block. A counterexample is X=I_3, f(X)=<A,X>, A=0.5*[[0,-1,1],[1,0,-1],[-1,1,0]], and h(X)=sum_i |sum_j X_ij-1|. Every exact two-row surrogate is minimized at the identity for Q=0 and theta>0, yet exp(-tA) is a feasible descent curve: h remains zero and the objective derivative is -||A||_F^2. Thus even exact block-2 stationarity need not imply criticality.

The strong-convergence proof contains independent substantive errors. Lemma 6.6(b) fails even for n=3, r=1, k=2, X=e_1, h=0, and f(X)=X_2: its left-hand side is 1, while its right-hand side is sqrt(2/3). The proof incorrectly converts a second-moment bound into a first-moment bound. Appendix B.10 also substitutes B^t for B^(t+1) inside an expectation despite X^(t+1) depending on B^t. These steps invalidate the supplied justification for Theorem 6.8.

The breakpoint solver is not globally exact as written. Lemma 7.1 omits angles with cos(angle)=0; even minimizing -sin(angle) requires such an angle. Section 7.1 also discards coordinates with y_i=0, although their l1 contribution lambda*|x_i|/sqrt(1+t^2) depends on t. Furthermore, zeros of x_i+t*y_i occur at -x_i/y_i, whereas the listed breakpoint sets use the opposite sign.

The approximate solver does not match the analyzed algorithm. Section 7.2 omits the proximal term theta*||V-I||_F^2/2 required by Equation (11). Finding a critical point of the unregularized restricted objective does not establish the criticality and sufficient-decrease conditions assumed for OBCD-Approx.

The experimental initialization is inconsistent with the reported feasibility. Section 9.1 sets each nonnegative column's active entries to 1/|G_i|, giving squared column norm 1/|G_i| rather than 1. Since OBCD preserves X^TX, this initialization cannot yield Table 5's near-machine-precision orthogonality without an unreported normalization.

Efficiency and reproducibility evidence is incomplete. Only OBCD's breakpoint routine receives a C++ implementation, confounding the MATLAB wall-clock comparisons. Repeated-run uncertainty, detailed baseline tuning, and a precise runnable code artifact are not provided. Giving baseline solutions an additional ten seconds of OBCD refinement also does not isolate an algorithmic advantage without equal-budget baseline continuation.

The incremental contribution over existing Givens-rotation coordinate descent is insufficiently isolated experimentally. There is no direct comparison with the cited closely related coordinate methods, no rotation-only versus rotation-plus-reflection ablation, and no comparison with the cited specialized exact-penalty methods for nonnegative orthogonality. Reducing two-row updates to rotations and reflections makes small subproblems tractable; the working-set heuristics are practically motivated.
Experiments cover four problem classes, ten datasets, multiple ranks and regularization settings, with relevant baselines and substantial reported improvements on several instances.

Thus approximate block stationarity need not imply criticality, even for a convex nonsmooth penalty and linear smooth term.

strengths: The row-wise orthogonal update is a useful algorithmic idea: it preserves feasibility and permits inexpensive partial-gradient updates for rectangular Stiefel problems.
The majorization construction supports sufficient decrease when subproblems are solved globally. Considering both rotations and reflections correctly covers both components of O(2).

Experiments cover ten datasets, three PCA formulations, several ranks and regularization strengths, and working-set variants. They report substantial objective improvements in many settings and include ManPG comparisons for ℓ1 regularization.
weaknesses: The central optimality claim, Theorem 3.6(a), is false under the stated assumptions. Appendix F.2 incorrectly replaces a potentially different subgradient for each block with one subgradient satisfying every block condition. A counterexample is b=1/√2, X=[[0,b],[b,1/2],[b,-1/2]], h(Y)=||Y||₁, f(Y)=⟨C,Y⟩ with C=[[0,b-1],[-1,-1],[-1,1]], H=Q=0, and α=1. Convexity of h certifies that I₂ globally minimizes every block majorizer: the corresponding supporting block matrices are diag(1/2,0), diag(1/2,0), and zero. Nevertheless, full criticality requires the subgradient at X₁₁=0 to equal both -1/2 and +1/2. Thus X is block-2 stationary but not critical, directly contradicting the advertised stronger-than-critical guarantee.

The convergence proofs contain additional substantive gaps. Equation (48), step 2, exchanges expectations over Bᵗ and Bᵗ⁺¹ even though Xᵗ⁺¹ depends on Bᵗ. Equation (54) incorrectly converts a second-moment identity into a first-moment identity. These steps do not establish the KL convergence result. Separately, Equation (42) bounds updates evaluated at different iterates during a cycle; it does not establish the claimed ε-block-stationarity of one common iterate in Theorem 4.2(c).

The exact breakpoint solver is incorrect as written. Section 5 and Appendix B identify zeros of xᵢ+t yᵢ using t=xᵢ/yᵢ instead of -xᵢ/yᵢ. Section 5 also discards coordinates with yᵢ=0, although their ℓ1 contribution λ|xᵢ|/√(1+t²) generally depends on t. These errors can change the minimizer and must be resolved before relying on exact subproblem solutions in the algorithm or proofs.

The claimed generality depends on Assumption (Asm-iii), which assumes exact, efficient global solution of the difficult nonsmooth orthogonal subproblem. Constructive nonsmooth solvers and experiments address k=2. The broader k>2 framework therefore lacks a demonstrated practical solver, and the assertion that merely finding critical subproblem points preserves convergence needs additional conditions and proof.

The empirical evidence needs stronger controls and reproducibility details. Randomized methods are reported without repeated-run variability; baseline tuning, data preprocessing, and sensitivity to α are insufficiently specified. Nonnegative PCA comparisons omit dedicated methods such as the cited Jiang et al. (2022). Warm-start improvements receive additional computation without equal-total-time continuation controls. Short objective-versus-time runs cannot establish the claim that competing methods remain trapped in local minima indefinitely. These limitations compound the fundamental theoretical problems and support a strong rejection in the present form.

Combining rotations and reflections offers a useful approach to nonsmooth updates without full-matrix retractions.

Experiments cover ten datasets and three PCA formulations, include ManPG for ℓ1 regularization, and report substantial objective improvements in several settings. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b06/review-experiment-f26y2exq/call-f88a5be8b8c24295b614d1a69fc7a661/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The central optimality claim, Theorem 3.6(a), is false as stated. Equations (31)–(32) replace a potentially different subgradient for each block with one common subgradient. A counterexample uses a=1/√2, X=[[0,a],[a,1/2],[a,-1/2]], h(Y)=∥Y∥₁, f(Y)=⟨A,Y⟩ with A=[[0,a−1],[-1,-1],[-1,1]], Q=0, and α=1. Identity globally minimizes every two-row surrogate: supporting linear matrices are diag(1/2,0) for blocks {1,2} and {1,3}, and zero for {2,3}. However, full subgradients are G_s=[[s,a],[0,0],[0,0]], s∈[-1,1], and min_s ∥G_s−XG_sᵀX∥_F=1/2. Thus a BS2 point need not even be critical, invalidating the advertised stronger-stationarity guarantee.

The KL convergence proof contains additional substantive errors. Equation (48), step ②, exchanges the previous and next sampled blocks despite X^(t+1) depending on the previous block. Equations (53)–(54) also convert a second-moment identity into a first-moment equality without justification and overlook block-dependent subgradient choices. Consequently, Theorem 4.8 is not established.

The cyclic complexity argument is incomplete. Equation (42) bounds update sizes evaluated at different iterates throughout a cycle, whereas Definition 4.1 requires all block residuals evaluated at one common iterate. The claimed implication to an ε-BSk point lacks the necessary residual-transfer argument.

The breakpoint solver is incorrect as written. Solving x_i+t y_i=0 requires t=−x_i/y_i, but Section 5 lists the positive ratio. Furthermore, discarding coordinates with y_i=0 is invalid for the ℓ1 extension: λ|x_i|/√(1+t²) still depends on t. These issues directly affect the exact-subproblem assumption underpinning the algorithm.

The empirical evidence has limited scope and uncertainty reporting. All applications are related PCA objectives with n≤1000 and k=2; repeated-run statistics and baseline tuning details are absent. Short time-budget comparisons cannot establish the Figure 1 claim that competitors remain trapped regardless of runtime. Every two-row orthogonal update has F(Y)≥F(X): rotation increments are bounded below by (q−1/2)|sin θ| for pairs involving row 1 and by zero otherwise; reflection increments are nonnegative. Considering both rotations and reflections covers both components of O(2); reducing two-row nonsmooth subproblems to scalar candidate searches is practically appealing.
The experiments cover ten datasets and three PCA formulations, with relevant baselines, runtime curves, and nonnegativity measurements.

Equations (51)–(52) exchange the previously selected block with a fresh random block although the evaluated matrix depends on the previous selection through X^(t+1). Equation (52) exchanges the previously selected block with a fresh independent block even though the updated iterate depends on the previous selection. strengths: OBCD’s row updates preserve orthogonality and permit partial-gradient computations. The sufficient-decrease argument under exact block minimization is a useful foundation.
Reducing two-row updates to rotations and reflections provides an attractive approach to separable nonsmooth penalties.
Experiments cover three PCA formulations and ten datasets with several relevant baselines. Table 3 reports substantial nonnegative-PCA objective improvements with negligible nonnegativity violations.
weaknesses: The central stationarity claim is false under the stated assumptions. A counterexample to Theorem 3.8(a) and Lemma 4.4(b) uses a=1/√2, X=[[0,a,a],[a,1/2,-1/2],[a,-1/2,1/2]], W=(a/2)[[0,1,-1],[-1,0,0],[1,0,0]], and F(Y)=〈WX/2−sign(X),Y〉+||Y||₁, with sign(0)=0. Appendix E.3 incorrectly replaces the existence of a potentially different subgradient for each block with the existence of one subgradient satisfying every block condition.

The stochastic convergence analysis has an independent dependency error. Equations (51)–(52) interchange averaging over Bᵗ and Bᵗ⁺¹ even though the matrix being averaged depends on Xᵗ⁺¹, hence on Bᵗ. Identical marginal sampling distributions do not justify this interchange. Appendix F.4 also applies expectation bounds as pointwise bounds. Consequently, the claimed criticality complexity and KL convergence guarantees are not established.

The main ℓ0-SPCA experiments test a regime with a closed-form solution. Appendix G.2 normalizes ||A||_F=1, implying tr(C)=1 and 0≤tr(XᵀCX)≤1. With every tested λ≥10, any feasible matrix having more than r nonzeros is worse than a matrix with exactly r nonzeros. The optimum therefore consists of signed coordinate vectors selecting the r largest diagonal entries of C. This elementary baseline is missing, and these experiments do not demonstrate performance on a substantive sparsity–variance tradeoff.

The ℓ1-SPCA comparisons initialize OBCD with an identity matrix while initializing every baseline randomly. This confounds algorithmic performance with initialization, particularly under the dominant sparsity penalties used here. Repeated-seed variability, baseline tuning details, reflection/majorizer ablations, and sparsity versus explained-variance results are also missing.

Appendix B contains errors in the claimed exact subproblem solver. The ℓ0 breakpoint list uses xᵢ/yᵢ although zeros of xᵢ+tyᵢ occur at −xᵢ/yᵢ. Discarding pairs with yᵢ=0 is also invalid for ℓ1 regularization because λ|xᵢ|/√(1+t²) still depends on t. The derivation and implementation require verification, since exact global subproblem solutions are essential to the guarantees.
